Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models route input tokens to specialized sub-networks (experts) via a learned gating function, and during fine-tuning on multiple objectives simultaneously, the gradient signal flowing back through that gate becomes a superposition of task-specific gradients weighted by their respective loss scales. The central question is whether this superposition causes the routing decisions to be systematically distorted — not toward what each expert is best at, but toward whichever task's loss dominates numerically, effectively re-specializing experts away from their pre-trained functional roles. Key concepts include load balancing auxiliary losses (which already compete with task losses), the geometry of gradient interference in the gate's parameter space, and the distinction between expert utilization collapse (most tokens going to one expert) and routing drift (gradients gradually reshaping which inputs go where in semantically meaningful but unintended ways). A beginner assumes that separate experts provide automatic isolation — that task A's gradient can't corrupt task B's expert — but this misses that the router itself is a shared, fully-differentiable bottleneck through which all task gradients pass simultaneously, and that expert outputs are linearly combined before the loss is computed, so even "inactive" experts receive gradient updates proportional to their gate weight.

Freezing the router eliminates routing drift — the gradual corruption of gate parameters by competing task gradients — and preserves whatever expert specialization emerged during pre-training, which matters most when the pre-trained router encodes hard-won load balance across a large expert pool (e.g., the 64-expert or 128-expert configurations in GShard or Switch Transformer, where rebalancing from scratch is expensive). The failure mode you introduce, however, is expert capacity mismatch under distribution shift: the frozen router was calibrated to a token distribution from pre-training, but fine-tuning tasks often have narrower, domain-specific token distributions, so tokens systematically crowd into a small subset of experts that the pre-trained gate associates with those inputs, while other experts receive near-zero gradient signal and go stale. This is strictly worse in one sense: routing drift is a slow corruption you can monitor and potentially regularize, but capacity mismatch is structural — the frozen gate actively funnels the fine-tuning signal into a few experts, and those experts must now absorb objectives they may not be individually suited for, collapsing multi-task diversity into a single overloaded subnetwork. Fedus et al. (Switch Transformers, 2022) noted that expert utilization entropy drops sharply on domain-specific data even with a trained router; a frozen router amplifies this because it cannot adapt even the small corrective adjustments that online routing would make. The deeper problem is that frozen routing converts a soft interference problem (gradients competing through a shared gate) into a hard allocation problem (some experts are structurally excluded from learning), and excluded experts can't be recovered by any downstream loss weighting scheme without unfreezing.

Loss normalization equalizes the scalar magnitudes of task gradients before they enter backpropagation, but at the expert output combination step, the problem is geometric rather than scalar: each expert produces a vector in residual stream space, and the gate weights determine a convex combination of those vectors that gets passed forward. When two tasks require different directions in that residual stream space — say, task A needs expert 3's output to point toward a syntactic feature subspace while task B needs a semantic one — the combined gradient pushes the gate weights toward a compromise combination that satisfies neither, and this interference happens after loss normalization has already done its work, inside the forward-pass arithmetic. Concretely, if the gate assigns weights [0.6, 0.3, 0.1] to three experts for a given token, the backward pass updates those weights based on how each expert's contribution reduced the joint loss, but the joint loss gradient at that combination point reflects the dot product between the residual stream direction the combination produced and the direction each task actually needed — and these can be nearly orthogonal regardless of how well-normalized the losses are. This is related to what Yu et al. (2020, "Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning") identified as gradient conflict — negative cosine similarity between task gradients — except in MoE the conflict is localized to the combination coefficients and is invisible to any loss-level intervention. Mixtral-style top-k routing (k=2) sharpens the problem: with only two active experts per token, the convex combination has very little degrees of freedom, so a geometric conflict between task requirements at a given layer has almost no slack to resolve — one task's gradient will dominate the gate update for that token by virtue of which direction in residual space is locally more curved, not which task loss was larger.

Gradient surgery projects each task's gradient onto the orthogonal complement of conflicting task gradients, but this requires computing pairwise gradient cosine similarities — an operation that assumes the parameter space is dense and continuous in the relevant region, which the gate parameters in top-k routing are not. In top-k sparse routing, the gate produces a discrete selection (e.g., top-2 of 64 experts), and the straight-through estimator or softmax-before-topk trick used to make this differentiable means the gate's "gradient" is actually a surrogate computed over the full softmax distribution, even though only k experts contributed to the forward pass — so you're projecting a gradient that doesn't accurately reflect the actual discrete routing decision. The projection itself then compounds the problem: when you remove the conflicting component of task B's gradient from task A's gate update, you may be zeroing out exactly the gate weight adjustments that would have increased utilization of a currently-underused expert, because the conflict signal and the load-balancing signal are entangled in the same parameter dimensions — Yu et al. noted that projection can reduce effective gradient magnitude by 30-70% in high-conflict regimes, and in sparse MoE that magnitude reduction disproportionately affects low-weight experts who already receive weak gradient signal. There's also a combinatorial explosion problem: with 64 experts and top-2 routing, there are 2016 possible expert pairs per token, and different tasks may conflict on different subsets of those pairs, so the "conflict graph" over gate parameters is not static — it changes with every batch depending on which tokens activate which pairs, making the projection target a moving surface that gradient surgery, designed for fixed parameter vectors, cannot track. Finally, gradient surgery operates on the gradient vector for a parameter, but the gate's effective gradient for a given expert slot is only nonzero when that expert was selected in the current batch, creating extreme sparsity in the gradient tensor that makes cosine similarity estimates statistically unreliable — you're measuring conflict between two vectors most of whose entries are zero for different reasons, which can produce spurious orthogonality or spurious conflict depending on batch composition.

The shifting conflict structure means that any gradient-modification scheme targeting the router faces a non-stationary optimization landscape in the precise technical sense: the effective loss surface seen by the gate parameters changes with each batch's expert selection pattern, which violates the stationarity assumptions underlying convergence proofs for SGD, Adam, and virtually all gradient-surgery variants. Yu et al.'s convergence proof for gradient surgery assumes the conflict graph is fixed or at least slowly varying relative to the learning rate schedule; in sparse MoE with stochastic top-k, the conflict graph can flip sign (from conflicting to aligned) within a single epoch as the router itself shifts which experts get selected, creating a situation where the modification scheme is chasing a target that moves faster than the optimizer converges. The practical implication is that per-batch gradient surgery on gate parameters doesn't just converge slowly — it can actively destabilize routing by making systematic updates based on conflict estimates that are stale by the next forward pass, and empirically this manifests as the load-balancing entropy collapsing and recovering in cycles rather than monotonically improving, a pattern visible in training curves from systems like ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022) even without explicit gradient surgery. The theoretical object that does remain stable across batches is the expected routing distribution — the marginal probability that a given expert handles a given input type, averaged over the data distribution — which is a property of the gate's parameters rather than any single batch's discrete selections, and changes only as fast as the parameters themselves change. This suggests targeting the Jacobian of the expected routing distribution with respect to gate parameters rather than the per-batch gradient: this Jacobian, which relates to the Fisher information matrix of the routing policy, averages out the stochastic selection noise and provides a stable geometric object that conflict-resolution schemes could project against — essentially treating the router as a stochastic policy and borrowing natural gradient methods from reinforcement learning, where exactly this non-stationarity problem was solved by TRPO and PPO through trust region constraints on policy change per update.

The trust region constraint bounds the KL divergence between the old and new routing distributions — effectively capping how much any token's expert assignment probabilities can shift per update — but the load-balancing auxiliary loss pushes gate parameters in whatever direction reduces expert utilization skew, regardless of whether that direction violates the KL bound. The tension is sharpest when the current routing distribution is already unbalanced: the auxiliary loss demands large parameter updates to redistribute tokens across underused experts, but the trust region says those updates would change the routing policy too drastically, so the constraint actively resists the rebalancing signal — and in practice, with typical auxiliary loss coefficients around 0.01-0.1 (as used in Switch Transformer and ST-MoE), the trust region radius (typically KL ≤ 0.01 in TRPO-style updates) will frequently be the binding constraint, meaning load balancing makes negligible progress per step. This creates a stage-dependent priority inversion: early in fine-tuning, the pre-trained router's distribution may be well-balanced but poorly matched to the new task distribution, so the trust region correctly slows routing drift while task-specific gradients accumulate in expert parameters — here the trust region should dominate. Later in fine-tuning, however, task gradients have reshaped which tokens flow where, and utilization skew has likely grown because certain experts are now systematically preferred by the narrowed task distribution; at this stage the auxiliary loss needs room to operate, meaning the trust region radius should be relaxed or the auxiliary loss coefficient increased, otherwise you get expert collapse that is irreversible without a full rebalancing phase. The deepest problem is that neither TRPO nor standard auxiliary loss formulations have a principled mechanism for this handoff — TRPO's radius is typically fixed or annealed on a schedule tied to policy return, not expert entropy, so you would need a adaptive trust region that widens specifically when utilization entropy drops below a threshold, essentially coupling the KL constraint to a routing health metric rather than to task loss curvature, which no current MoE system implements explicitly.

The least destructive architectural intervention is selective gate re-initialization with representation-preserving expert cloning: identify the overloaded experts (those handling >2x their fair share of tokens), clone their weights into the underutilized experts (which have near-zero utilization and therefore near-random, stale weights anyway), then reinitialize only the gate's output logits for the underutilized experts with small random perturbations around the overloaded expert's gate score. This works because the underutilized experts' representations are already corrupted by gradient starvation — they've received essentially no meaningful updates — so replacing their weights with a clone of a well-trained expert loses nothing, while giving the gate a nearby-but-distinct target to route to, allowing it to gradually differentiate the clones through subsequent fine-tuning updates. The key surgical precision is in what you do not touch: the overloaded expert's weights remain unchanged, the gate weights for all other experts remain unchanged, and you only perturb the logit bias terms (if the architecture has them, as in Expert Choice routing) or add a small learned per-expert temperature scalar — a single parameter per expert — that shifts effective gate scores without altering the residual stream geometry the task representations depend on. This is structurally similar to what Komatsuzaki et al. (2022, "Sparse Upcycling") did when initializing MoE models from dense checkpoints — copying dense FFN weights into multiple experts and relying on subsequent training to differentiate them — except applied locally to a subset of experts mid-training rather than globally at initialization. The risk is that cloned experts initially produce identical outputs for identical inputs, giving the gate zero gradient signal to differentiate between them for several hundred steps; this can be mitigated by adding a small noise vector to the cloned expert's input projection weights (not output, to preserve the representation subspace the gate is targeting) with magnitude around 0.01-0.05 of the weight norm, which breaks symmetry while keeping the expert's effective function close enough to the original that the gate's existing routing logic remains valid.

The property you need to verify is intra-expert token heterogeneity: the set of tokens currently routed to the overloaded expert must contain at least two distinguishable subpopulations whose optimal processing directions in residual stream space are sufficiently separated that a small perturbation in expert weights will cause the gate to preferentially route one subpopulation to the original and the other to the clone. If all tokens routed to the overloaded expert require nearly the same transformation — which happens when collapse is caused by a narrow fine-tuning distribution rather than genuine multi-functionality — then no amount of perturbation will produce divergence, because the gradient signal from both subpopulations pushes both experts in the same direction, and the clones re-converge within a few hundred steps regardless of initialization noise. The granularity at which you need to verify this is the token embedding cluster structure within the expert's activation space: concretely, you would run k-means or a GMM on the hidden states of tokens routed to that expert (at the layer just before the MoE block), and check whether the resulting clusters have inter-cluster distance significantly larger than intra-cluster variance — a silhouette score above roughly 0.3 is a reasonable empirical threshold, though this number is not yet standardized in the MoE literature. If the clusters exist, you also need to verify that the gate's current weight vector is not already aligned with the cluster centroid difference vector — if it is, the gate already "wants" to separate them but is prevented by capacity constraints, and a simple capacity increase would suffice; if it isn't, the perturbation needs to be directionally aligned with that centroid difference to have any chance of seeding divergence rather than just adding noise. Anthropic's published work on superposition and feature geometry suggests that in large transformers, individual MLP layers (and by extension MoE experts) frequently encode hundreds of near-orthogonal features simultaneously, which implies that token heterogeneity within an overloaded expert is the norm rather than the exception in general-purpose models — but domain-specific fine-tuning actively destroys this heterogeneity by narrowing the input distribution, which is precisely why you cannot assume clones will diverge without measuring cluster structure in the fine-tuned activation space, not the pre-trained one.
